problem: Prior instruction-following work maps language to low-level motions or formal grammars, or uses a two-step generate-then-verify pipeline. Neither exploits a high-level topological map of the environment as a knowledge base to resolve ambiguous, incomplete free-form instructions.
motivation: Free-form navigation instructions are highly variable and often omit actions or imply behaviors, for example 'advance forward' may or may not include crossing intersections. Resolving this needs environment structure. The observation is that a behavioral navigation graph of <node, edge, node> triplets can act like a knowledge base that attention correlates with the instruction, as in QA and retrieval.
key_idea: Encode the behavioral navigation graph as triplets, attend from each triplet to instruction words, and decode a behavior sequence with a graph-connectivity mask, all end-to-end.
insight: Feeding the graph as a knowledge base helps considerably: in Test-Repeated, Ablation with Mask reaches EM 45.95 versus 57.31 for Ours with Mask. The output-mask constraint helps in both test sets, e.g. Ours without Mask gets EM 21.94 in Test-New versus 38.52 with Mask. Ordering triplets starting from the start location gives a further gain, EM 61.17 and 41.71. Generalization to new environments remains weak. Correct predictions on hand-collected sub-optimal routes suggest the model uses the instructions rather than only shortest paths.
method: Embed layer: instruction words use 100-d GloVe; graph triplets (p_i, b_l[attr], p_j) are one-hot encoded, each component of dimension 2N+E.
Encoder layer: two independent bidirectional GRUs (hidden size 128) encode the instruction and the triplet sequence into I-bar (T x 2H) and G-bar (L x 2H).
Attention layer: one-way attention where each triplet attends over instruction words (e_i = G_i W I^T, softmax). The weighted sum R_i is concatenated with G_i to give F_i=[R_i;G_i].
FC layer: reduces each F_i from 4H to H, forming the context matrix C.

Decoder layer: a GRU takes the previous behavior (start node as initial input) and attends over C (additive attention, Eqs. 4-5). The resulting context S_t and h_t give logits o_t=W3[S_t;h_t] over behaviors plus a stop symbol.
Output layer: masks logits using graph connectivity from the current node n_t (0 for valid behaviors and stop, -inf otherwise) before argmax, guaranteeing valid paths.
Ordered Triplets: triplets around the robot's start location are presented first instead of alphabetical order, to help localize the start.
Dataset: 11,051 instruction-plan pairs (8066 train, Test-Repeated 1012, Test-New 962) collected on Mechanical Turk over 100 simulated maps, each with 6-65 rooms.

setting.backbone: Bidirectional GRU encoders + attention + GRU decoder (trained from scratch, GloVe embeddings)
setting.training_data: 8066 instruction-plan pairs from 88 simulated environments (Mechanical Turk); 12.5% held out for validation
setting.observation: Text instruction + topological behavioral graph (triplets) + known start node; no visual input
setting.action_space: High-level behaviors (edges of the behavioral graph: 11 types such as oo<d>, io<d>, cf, <d>t, sp, ch<d>)
setting.simulator: Simulated topological indoor maps (custom dataset, no physics simulator)
setting.privileged: Ground-truth behavioral navigation graph of the environment and the start node are given as input

numbers_note: The dataset is the paper's own and not a canonical benchmark, so the split is labelled 'test' for both Test-Repeated and Test-New; they are distinguished in eval_set_note.
results: The full model (Mask + Ordered Triplets) gets EM 61.17 / GM 61.36 on Test-Repeated and EM 41.71 / GM 41.81 on Test-New. This beats the two-step Baseline (EM 25.30 / 25.44) and the map-free Ablation with Mask (45.95 / 36.45). Performance drops markedly in new environments, but the model is still about 3% EM/GM better than the second-best model there.
limitations: Large generalization gap between seen and unseen environments (EM 61 to 42).
Assumes a given ground-truth topological behavioral graph and known start; data are simulated with crowd-sourced, ambiguous instructions, and graphs are truncated to 300 triplets.
No robot execution or visual perception; only shortest-path routes in the dataset, with sub-optimal paths tested on just a few examples.
